HR@10 with one positive and 99 negatives measures success within a 100-item candidate set. Sampled metrics can reverse model orderings relative to full-catalog evaluation, even in expectation; narrower confidence intervals cannot remove this bias. Interpret gains as improvements on the pinned sampled benchmark, without claiming equivalent full-catalog gains. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For this design, compare models using paired per-user hit differences on identical users and candidates. Bootstrap user pairs within each category, preserving 200 users/category, then recompute the equally weighted four-category mean; report a 95% interval for the difference and category-level effects. Paired randomization provides a complementary test. Bootstrap and randomization have established support in recommendation evaluation. One changed hit moves category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points: small gains may represent very few users. These intervals are conditional on fitted models, fixed candidates and seeds; they do not measure training-seed or negative-sampling variability, nor generalization across datasets. [Ihemelandu and Ekstrand](https://piret.info/pubs/2023/SIGIR23-InferenceAtScale)

Repeated checkpoint and hyperparameter selection on the same validation users creates optimistic selection bias; a confidence interval computed only for the selected winner does not account for the search. Log every evaluated configuration/checkpoint, disclose selection effort, and treat small validation gains as exploratory. Multiplicity adjustments can support prespecified comparisons but do not fully repair adaptive reuse. Independent evaluation after freezing selection is the strongest confirmation; here, preserve the pinned evaluator and seeds and reserve held-out evaluation for the host’s final step. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
